work.title: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection
work.rights: Project Gutenberg identifies the 1859 first edition as public domain in the USA.

scope_read: First-edition title page, introduction, contents, and opening section on variation under domestication. Compared with the sixth edition's retrospective historical sketch.
historical_context: Darwin's introduction locates the problem in observations of the geographical distribution of South American organisms and geological relations between living and fossil forms during the Beagle voyage.

Darwin states that he began systematic accumulation and reflection on relevant facts in 1837, drafted notes after five years, expanded a sketch in 1844, and continued the investigation before publishing in 1859.
He describes Alfred Russel Wallace's independently reached near-similar conclusions and the role of Charles Lyell and Joseph Dalton Hooker in arranging joint communication of the 1858 papers.

Darwin situates the theory among existing disputes about species immutability and earlier proposals of species modification; the sixth edition later expands this history and acknowledges additional predecessors.
Darwin explicitly says the 1859 volume is an abstract, that it cannot provide all references or balance every fact in detail, and that further publication of evidence is needed.
what_darwin_did: Combined observations from biogeography, geology, domestication, variation, classification, embryology and the fossil record into a common explanatory framework.
Used domestic breeding as an accessible analogue for selection and cumulative inherited variation, then asked how selection could operate in nature.
Applied the struggle-for-existence argument associated with Malthus to population growth and differential survival and reproduction.
Organized the book to address difficult objections, including transitional forms, instinct, hybridism and gaps in the geological record.
Named collaborators and predecessors and acknowledged the limits of his short-form presentation.

methodological_reading.note: Darwin gives a research chronology and explains why he is publishing an abstract before the full evidential treatment is complete.
The account makes scientific priority and communication part of the historical record, rather than presenting discovery as an isolated event.
Darwin openly states that facts may appear to support opposite conclusions and that the short book cannot fully balance every side.
He links geographical distribution, embryology, geological succession, mutual affinities and domestication.
He begins with breeders' observations, inherited differences, selection and the complexity of variation before moving to natural populations.
Darwin retrospectively discusses earlier thinkers including Buffon, Lamarck, Wells, Matthew and Wallace. This later account must not be confused with the 1859 first-edition text.

pioneer_questions: What observation first made the origin of species a live research problem for Darwin?
Why did he spend years collecting evidence before publishing?
How did domestication and breeding provide a model for thinking about natural selection?
Which neighboring disciplines supplied independent evidence?
How did he handle priority, collaboration, uncertainty and objections?
What changed between the first and sixth editions, and why is edition history scientifically informative?
cautions: Darwin's 1859 terminology and Victorian social context require historical analysis; do not treat period language as current scientific or ethical categories.
The theory's historical development involved predecessors and independent work, including Wallace; avoid lone-genius simplification.
Later genetics, molecular biology and the modern evolutionary synthesis were not available to Darwin in 1859.
